newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Maruti prepares to take on competition.
newsitem.headline: India's Maruti prepares to take on competition.

text.p: India's largest car maker Maruti Udyog Ltd claims it is firmly in the driver's seat and confident of warding off challenges posed by the new entrants in the domestic market.
Many global car makers, including Korea's Daewoo Corp, Germany's Daimler Benz, General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co of the U.S. have set up joint ventures in India in the last two years.
India opened up its domestic car market in 1993 as part of an economic reforms programme launched in 1991 after decades of socialist control.
"We have a share of 81 percent of the car market," R.C. Bhargava, managing director of Maruti, told Reuters in an interview.
Maruti is a joint venture between the Indian government and Japan's Suzuki Motor Corp The two are equal partners.
"In the small car segment there is absolutely no competition so far," said Bhargava, who has been with the company for about 16 years.

In the Indian market, cars priced below 400,000 rupees ($11,173) make up the economy or small car segment of the market, while cars costing between 400,000 and 700,000 rupees belong to the mid-sized segment, industry officials said.
Maruti first sold its 800 cc hatchback in December 1983 and later added two mid-sized cars -- the 1,000 cc Maruti 1000 and the 1,300 cc Maruti Esteem.
A family van, a "Gypsy" off-road vehicle and a higher grade hatchback Zen were also added to its stable.
In the initial years, Maruti with its 800 cc small car faced little competition in the domestic market.
"It was a very easy situation in the sense that the absence of competition made marketing and general operations very simple," Bhargava said.
In 1987 Maruti decided to start exporting to help make its workforce aware of the needs of a fiercely competitive global car market.
"That was a very useful way of ensuring that we didn't fall into the trap of becoming very complacent," Bhargava said.
The company, which sold only a few hundred cars in the world market in 1987, exported 26,000 cars in 1995/96 (April-March).
Bhargava admits that competition, even in the small car segment, is imminent but says the firm is ready.
"It will be difficult for any new car maker to upstage Maruti," said an automobile analyst with a foreign securities firm who asked not to be identified.
Most of the new players are in the mid-size or larger car segment, he said, adding there were very few firms planning to produce small cars.
"I think we have lot of strength in terms of our volumes, brand image, local content, vendor base, dealer network," Bhargava said.
"We have strength in having Suzuki as our partner."
Industry analysts say Suzuki is also keen to consolidate its position in the Indian market, particularly with the entry of several foreign car makers.
Last year Maruti approved a 15 billion rupee ($419 million) expansion plan to add 100,000 units to its existing capacity of 250,000 vehicles at its factory on the outskirts of New Dehli.
The funds for expansion will come from internal resources and debt. The new capacity is likely to be commissioned by the end of 1998.
"My problem is, in the next two years I don't have the capacity for growth," Bhargava said, adding the company planned to consolidate its business in 1997 and 1998.
"So the best we can do in this period is to improve quality, work to reduce cost, improve the marketing network and generally consolidate," he said.
In the current fiscal year ending on March 31, the company expects to produce about 335,000 vehicles compared with 276,000 a year earlier.

Maruti is currently operating at about 40 percent above its capacity of 250,000 cars per year. A company official said it had been able to stretch existing capacity as "increased productivity has enabled us to improve capacity utilisation".
After capacity expansion, the company expects to produce 500,000 vehicles by the year 2000.
With a net profit of 4.09 billion rupees in 1995/96 compared with 2.48 billion in the previous year, Bhargava says the small car segment will continue to dominate the domestic market.
"As and when the market for bigger cars grows...we will certainly look at going into the bigger car segment," he said.
